**Indian National Physics Olympiad – 2019**

Date: 03 February 2019. Time: **09:00–12:00 (3 hours)**. Maximum Marks: **75**.

Roll Number: $1\,9\,\square\,\square-\square\,\square\,\square\,\square-\square\,\square\,\square\,\square$. Extra sheets attached: [blank box]. Centre (e.g. Kota): [blank line].

**(Do not write below this line)**

1. This booklet consists of 29 pages (excluding this page) and total of 7 questions.
2. This booklet is divided in two parts: **Questions with Summary Answer Sheet** and **Detailed Answer Sheet**. Write roll number at the top wherever asked.
3. **The final answer to each sub-question should be neatly written in the box provided below each sub-question in the Questions & Summary Answer Sheet.**
4. You are also required to show your detailed work for each question in a reasonably neat and coherent way in the **Detailed Answer Sheet**. You must write the relevant Question Number(s) on each of these pages.
5. Marks will be awarded on the basis of what you write on both the Summary Answer Sheet and the Detailed Answer Sheet. Simple short answers and plots may be directly entered in the Summary Answer Sheet. Marks may be deducted for absence of detailed work in questions involving longer calculations. Strike out any rough work that you do not want to be considered for evaluation.
6. Adequate space has been provided in the answersheet for you to write/calculate your answers. In case you need extra space to write, you may request additional blank sheets from the invigilator. Write your roll number on the extra sheets and get them attached to your answersheet and indicate number of extra sheets attached at the top of this page.
7. Non-programmable scientific calculators are allowed. Mobile phones **cannot** be used as calculators.
8. Use blue or black pen to write answers. Pencil may be used for diagrams/graphs/sketches.

problems.title: Propagation of sound
problems.statement:
In the lower part of the earth’s atmosphere, the temperature decreases with increase of height. Choose the origin of the coordinate system at the ground level with the $y$-axis vertically upward and the $x$-axis horizontal. We assume a linear decrease of temperature such that the temperature at a height $y$ from the ground level is

$$T(y)=T_0(1-by)$$

where $T_0$ is the temperature at the ground level. The constant $b=0.023\ \mathrm{km^{-1}}$. We consider the propagation of sound in the $x$-$y$ plane. Ignore any attenuation, reflection, and diffraction of sound.

**Native answer booklet:** PDF pages10–26 and30 (printed pages9–25 and29) are eighteen blank Detailed Answers pages with a “Que. No.” box and, on alternate printed pages, a “Last four digits of Roll No.:” field. The complete original remains available; its first blank answer-page template is retained here.

[[figure:p1-answer-template]]

parts.label: a)
parts.statement:
If $v_0$ is the speed of sound at the ground level, obtain an expression for the speed of sound $v(y)$ at height $y$, in terms of $v_0$ and $b$.

**Summary answer box:** $v(y)=$ [blank].

parts.label: b)
parts.statement:
Suppose sound propagates from the origin with an initial angle $\theta_0$ with the $x$-axis. Obtain an expression for the angle $\theta$ made by the direction of propagation of sound with the horizontal at height $y$, in terms of $\theta_0$ and $b$.

**Summary answer box:** $\theta=$ [blank].

parts.label: c)
parts.statement:
Obtain an expression for the $x$ and $y$ coordinates of a point on the path of propagation as functions of $\theta$.

**Summary answer boxes:** $x=$ [blank]; $y=$ [blank].

parts.label: d)
parts.statement:
For this part assume the direction of propagation of sound to be horizontal at the origin. For the case where $y$ is of the order $100\ \mathrm m$ or less, obtain an approximated expression relating $x$ and $y$ i.e. $y(x)$. Obtain $x$ for $y=2.00\ \mathrm m$.

**Summary answer boxes:** $y(x)=$ [blank]; Value of $x=$ [blank].

Detailed answers can be found on page numbers: [blank].

figures.alt: Whole first blank native Detailed Answers sheet, printed page9, blank question-number box and complete answer frame.

solution.statement:
### (a)

Speed of sound is

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{m}}\tag{1.1}$$

where $m$ and $\gamma$ are the molar mass and adiabatic index of the gas respectively.

$$v(y)=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT(y)}m}=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT_0}m}\sqrt{1-by}=v_0\sqrt{1-by}\tag{1.2}$$

Here $v_0=\sqrt{\gamma RT_0/m}$ is the speed of the sound at ground level.

### (b)

Consider the propogation of sound ‘ray’ from one medium to the other.

[[figure:p1-key-ray]]

From Snell’s law

$$\frac{\sin i_2}{\sin i_1}=\frac{v_2}{v_1}\tag{1.3}$$

$$\frac{\sin(\pi/2-\theta_2)}{\sin(\pi/2-\theta_1)}=\frac{\cos\theta_2}{\cos\theta_1}=\frac{v_2}{v_1}\tag{1.4}$$

$$\frac{\cos\theta}{\cos\theta_0}=\frac{v(y)}{v_0}=\sqrt{1-by}\tag{1.5}$$

$$\theta=\cos^{-1}\left[\cos\theta_0\sqrt{1-by}\right]\tag{1.6}$$

### (c)

$$y=\frac1b\left(1-\frac{\cos^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta_0}\right)\tag{1.7}$$

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\tan\theta\tag{1.8}$$

$$dx=\frac{2\cos\theta\sin\theta}{\tan\theta\,b\cos^2\theta_0}\,d\theta\tag{1.9}$$

$$x=\int_0^x dx=\frac1{2b\cos^2\theta_0}\left[2(\theta-\theta_0)+\sin2\theta-\sin2\theta_0\right]\tag{1.10}$$

### (d)

For $y\le100\ \mathrm m$ and $\theta_0=0$, Eq. (1.6) gives $\theta\approx3^\circ$ (very small).

$$y\approx\frac1b\left[1-\left(1-\frac{\theta^2}{2}\right)^2\right]=\frac1b\theta^2\tag{1.11}$$

$$x\approx\frac1{2b}(2\theta+2\theta)=\frac{2\theta}b\tag{1.12}$$

$$x^2=\frac{4y}b\tag{1.13}$$

$$x(y=2)\approx590\ \mathrm m\tag{1.14}$$

Accepted range: $585$–$600\ \mathrm m$.

figures.alt: Entire native sound-ray refraction sketch with interface, dashed normal, incident/transmitted arrows, i1/i2 and theta1/theta2.

problems.title: Particle in a one dimensional box
problems.statement: Consider a particle of mass $m$ confined to a one dimensional box of length $L$. The particle moves in the box with momentum $p$ colliding elastically with the walls. We consider the quantum mechanics of this system. As far as possible, express your answers in terms of $\alpha=h^2/8m$.

parts.label: a)
parts.statement:
At each energy state, the particle may be represented by a standing wave given by the de Broglie hypothesis. Express its wavelengths $\lambda_{\mathrm{dB}}$ in terms of $L$ in the $n$th energy state.

**Summary answer box:** $\lambda_{\mathrm{dB}}=$ [blank].

parts.label: b)
parts.statement:
Write the energy of the $n$th energy state, $E_n$.

**Summary answer box:** $E_n=$ [blank].

parts.label: c)
parts.statement:
Let there be $N$ (mass $m$) electrons in this box where $N$ is an even number. Obtain the expression for the lowest possible total energy $U_0$ of the system (e.g., the ground state energy of this $N$-particle system). Neglect coulombic interaction between the electrons.

**Summary answer box:** $U_0=$ [blank].

parts.label: d)
parts.statement:
Express the total energy $U_1$ in terms of $U_0$ and relevant quantities when the system is in the first excited state. Also express the total energy $U_2$ in terms of $U_0$ and relevant quantities when the system is in the second excited state.

**Summary answer boxes:** $U_1=$ [blank]; $U_2=$ [blank].

parts.label: e)
parts.statement:
When the system is in the ground state, let the length of the box change slowly from $L$ to $L-\Delta L$. Obtain the magnitude of the force $F$ on each wall in terms of $U_0$, when $\Delta L\ll L$.

**Summary answer box:** $F=$ [blank].

parts.label: f)
parts.statement:
Assuming $N$ is large ($N\gg1$) obtain the ratio $r$ of $dU_0/dN$ to the energy level of the highest occupied ground state.

**Summary answer box:** $r=$ [blank].

parts.label: g)
parts.statement:
We assume once again that $N$ is large. Consider the possibility of the electrons forming a uniform continuum of length $L$ with constant linear density. Using dimensional analysis, calculate the gravitational energy of this system $U_G$ assuming that it depends on its total mass, universal gravitational constant $G$ and $L$. Equate this (attractive) energy to the (repulsive) energy $U_0(N)$. Obtain $L$ in terms of $N$ and related quantities.

**Summary answer boxes:** $U_G=$ [blank]; $L=$ [blank].

Detailed answers can be found on page numbers: [blank].

solution.statement:
### (a)

$$\lambda_{\mathrm{dB}}=\frac{2L}{n}$$

### (b)

$$E_n=\frac{p^2}{2m}=\frac{n^2h^2}{8mL^2}=\frac{\alpha n^2}{L^2}\tag{2.1}$$

where $p=h/\lambda_{\mathrm{dB}}$.

### (c)

Highest occupied energy level is $n_{\max}=N/2$ as each energy level is occupied by two electrons.

$$U_0=\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}E_n=\frac{2\alpha}{L^2}\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}n^2=\frac{\alpha N(N+1)(N+2)}{12L^2}\tag{2.2}$$

**Source note:** The first sum in printed Eq. (2.2) has no factor2 even though the adjacent text gives two electrons per level and the following sum has $2\alpha/L^2$. The complete printed equality is retained.

### (d)

1st excited state configuration is

[[figure:p2-key-first-configuration]]

$$U_1=U_0-\frac\alpha{L^2}\left(\frac N2\right)^2+\frac\alpha{L^2}\left(\frac N2+1\right)^2\tag{2.3}$$

$$=U_0+\frac\alpha{L^2}(N+1)\tag{2.4}$$

2nd excited state configuration is

[[figure:p2-key-second-configuration]]

$$U_2=U_0-\frac\alpha{L^2}\left(\frac N2-1\right)^2+\frac\alpha{L^2}\left(\frac N2+1\right)^2\tag{2.5}$$

$$=U_0+\frac\alpha{L^2}2N\tag{2.6}$$

### (e)

From the work-energy theorem,

$$F\Delta L=U_{\mathrm{final}}-U_{\mathrm{initial}}\tag{2.7}$$

$$=\frac{\alpha N(N+1)(N+2)}{12}\left[\frac1{(L-\Delta L)^2}-\frac1{L^2}\right]\tag{2.8}$$

$$F\approx\frac{\alpha N(N+1)(N+2)2}{12L^3}=\frac{2U_0}{L}\tag{2.9}$$

### (f)

$$\frac{dU_0}{dN}=\frac\alpha{12L^2}\frac d{dN}(N^3+3N^2+2N)\tag{2.10}$$

$$\approx\frac\alpha{12L^2}3N^2\tag{2.11}$$

Highest occupied ground state corresponds to $N/2$, for which the energy level is $\alpha N^2/4L^2$. Thus

$$r=1\tag{2.12}$$

### (g)

$$[U_G]=\frac{GM^2}L=\frac{GN^2m^2}L\quad\text{or}\quad-\frac{GN^2m^2}L$$

For large $N$, $U_0\approx\alpha N^3/12L^2$.

$$\frac{GN^2m^2}L=\frac{\alpha N^3}{12L^2}\tag{2.13}$$

$$L=\frac{\alpha N^3}{12GM^2}=\frac{Nh^2}{96Gm^3}\tag{2.14}$$

figures.alt: Full native first-excited configuration, energy-level labels N/2+1 and N/2, occupancy arrows and dashed levels.
Full native second-excited configuration, N/2+1,N/2,N/2-1 labels and all occupancy arrows.

problems.title: A chain
problems.statement:
A chain of length $l$ and linear density $\lambda$ hangs from a horizontal support with both ends A and B fixed to a horizontal support as shown. The two fixed ends are close to each other. At time $t=0$ the end A is released. All vertical distances ($x$) are measured with respect to the horizontal support with the downward direction taken as positive (A and B are initially at $x=0$).

[[figure:p3-chain]]

parts.label: a)
parts.statement:
Obtain the momentum $P$ of the center of mass of the system when the end A has fallen by a distance $x$, in terms of $x$ and speed $\dot x$.

**Summary answer box:** $P=$ [blank].

parts.label: b)
parts.statement:
Assume that the end A is falling freely under gravity, i.e., $\ddot x=g$. Obtain the tension $T$ at the fixed end B just before the chain completes the fall and becomes entirely vertical.

**Summary answer box:** $T=$ [blank].

Experimentally, the value of tension is found to be different from the above result. We adopt an alternative approach assuming conservation of mechanical energy.

parts.label: c)
parts.statement:
Obtain the potential energy $U(x)$ of the chain and plot it versus $x$. Take the potential energy of a point mass placed at the horizontal support to be zero.

[[figure:p3-blank-u]]

parts.label: d)
parts.statement:
Obtain the speed $\dot x$ when the end A has fallen by a distance $x$. Assume that all sections of the falling (right side) part of the chain have the same speed.

**Summary answer box:** $\dot x=$ [blank].

parts.label: e)
parts.statement:
Hence obtain $T(x)$ at B as a function of $x$ and related quantities. You are advised to simplify your expression as far as possible.

**Summary answer box:** $T(x)=$ [blank].

parts.label: f)
parts.statement:
Qualitatively sketch $T(x)$ versus $x$.

[[figure:p3-blank-t]]

Detailed answers can be found on page numbers: [blank].

figures.alt: Both original chain configurations t=0/t>0, supports, A/B endpoints, l/2 and x arrows.
Entire native blank answer/plot frame for the chain potential-energy request.
Full original blank T(x) versus x axes and response frame.

solution.statement:
### (a)

Let total mass of the chain to be $M=\lambda l$.

The mass of the left side of the chain $=\lambda\left(\frac{l+x}{2}\right)$.

CM of the left side of the chain $=\left(\frac{l+x}{4}\right)$.

The mass of the right side of the chain $=\lambda\left(\frac{l-x}{2}\right)$.

CM of the right side of the chain $=\left(x+\frac{l-x}{4}\right)$.

$$x_{\mathrm{CM}}=\frac{\lambda\left(\frac{l+x}2\right)\left(\frac{l+x}4\right)+\lambda\left(\frac{l-x}2\right)\left(x+\frac{l-x}4\right)}{\lambda l}\tag{3.1}$$

$$\lambda l x_{\mathrm{CM}}=\frac{\lambda l^2}4+\frac{\lambda lx}2-\frac{\lambda x^2}4\tag{3.2}$$

$$P=\lambda l\dot x_{\mathrm{CM}}=\lambda\left(\frac{l-x}2\right)\dot x\tag{3.3}$$

### (b)

$$\ddot x=g\tag{3.4}$$

$$\dot x=gt=\sqrt{2gx}\tag{3.5}$$

$$\dot P=Mg-T\tag{3.6}$$

From Eq. (3.3)

$$\dot P=\frac\lambda2\left[\ddot x(l-x)-\dot x^2\right]\tag{3.7}$$

$$\frac\lambda2[gl-3gx]=Mg-T\tag{3.8}$$

$$T(x)=\frac{Mg}2\left(1+\frac{3x}l\right)=\frac{\lambda lg}2\left(1+\frac{3x}l\right)\tag{3.9}$$

$$T(x=l)=2\lambda lg\tag{3.10}$$

Experimentally, the value of tension is found to be different from the above result. We adopt an alternative approach assuming conservation of mechanical energy.

### (c)

In general, $U=-\lambda lgx_{\mathrm{CM}}$. Using Eq. (3.2)

$$U=\frac{-\lambda g}4(l^2+2lx-x^2)\tag{3.11}$$

[[figure:p3-key-u]]

### (d)

From Eq. (3.3), kinetic energy of the chain

$$K(x)=\frac12\lambda\left(\frac{l-x}2\right)\dot x^2\tag{3.12}$$

As the total energy is conserved,

$$U(x)+K(x)=U(t=0)\tag{3.13}$$

$$\dot x^2=\left[\frac{g(2lx-x^2)}{(l-x)}\right]^{1/2}\tag{3.14}$$

$$\dot x=\left[\frac{g(2lx-x^2)}{(l-x)}\right]^{1/2}\tag{3.15}$$

**Source note:** Printed Eq. (3.14) has $\dot x^2$ on the left and a square-root exponent on the right; the next Eq. (3.15) repeats that right-hand side with $\dot x$ on the left. Both original equations are retained.

### (e)

$$\frac d{dt}\dot x^2=2\dot x\ddot x$$

Substituing Eq. (3.15) in the above equation yields

$$\ddot x=g+\frac{g(2lx-x^2)}{2(l-x)^2}\tag{3.16}$$

Combining Eqs. (3.6), (3.7) and (3.16)

$$T=\lambda lg-\frac\lambda2\left[\ddot x(l-x)-\dot x^2\right]\tag{3.17}$$

$$=\frac{\lambda g}{4(l-x)}[2l^2+2lx-3x^2]\tag{3.18}$$

### (f)

[[figure:p3-key-t]]

**Source note:** Both original key plots mark the chain endpoint with uppercase $L$; the question and key formulas define the chain length as lowercase $l$. The actual native plots are retained.

figures.alt: Entire native potential-energy graph, all axes, 0,L endpoint and both negative lambda g l squared levels.
Entire original T versus x curve with lambda g l/2 intercept, 0,L, asymptote and all labels.

problems.title: A compressible liquid
problems.statement:
Consider a long narrow cylinder of cross section $A$ filled with a compressible liquid up to height $h$ whose density $\rho$ is a function of the pressure $P(z)$ as $\rho(z)=\frac{\rho_0}{2}\left(1+\frac{P(z)}{P_0}\right)$ where $P_0$ and $\rho_0$ are constants. The depth $z$ is measured from the free surface of the liquid where the pressure is equal to the atmospheric pressure ($P_{\mathrm{atm}}$).

[[figure:p4-cylinder]]

parts.label: a)
parts.statement:
Obtain the pressure ($P(z)$) as a function of $z$. Obtain the mass ($M$) of liquid in the tube.

**Summary answer boxes:** $P(z)=$ [blank]; $M=$ [blank].

parts.label: b)
parts.statement:
Let $P_i(z)$ be the pressure at $z$, if the liquid were incompressible with density $\rho_0/2$. Assuming that $P_0\gg\rho_0gz$ obtain an approximated expression for $\Delta P=P(z)-P_i(z)$.

**Summary answer box:** $\Delta P\approx$ [blank].

Detailed answers can be found on page numbers: [blank].

figures.alt: Complete original cylinder, liquid free surface, h/z dimensions, atmospheric-pressure label and downward g arrow.

solution.statement:
### (a)

$$P(z)=\int\rho(z)g\,dz+P_{\mathrm{atm}}\tag{4.1}$$

$$=\int_0^z\frac{\rho_0}2\left(1+\frac{P(z)}{P_0}\right)g\,dz+P_{\mathrm{atm}}\tag{4.2}$$

$$\frac{dP(z)}{dz}=\frac{\rho_0}2\left(1+\frac{P(z)}{P_0}\right)g\tag{4.3}$$

$$\int_{P_{\mathrm{atm}}}^{P(z)}\frac{dP(z)}{P_0+P(z)}=\int_0^z\frac{\rho_0g\,dz}{2P_0}\tag{4.4}$$

$$\log\frac{P_0+P(z)}{P_0+P_{\mathrm{atm}}}=\frac{\rho_0gz}{2P_0}\tag{4.5}$$

$$P(z)=\left[(P_0+P_{\mathrm{atm}})e^{\rho_0gz/2P_0}-P_0\right]\tag{4.6}$$

$$\rho(z)=\frac{\rho_0(P_0+P_{\mathrm{atm}})}{2P_0}e^{\rho_0gz/2P_0}\tag{4.7}$$

$$M=\int_0^h\rho(z)A\,dz\tag{4.8}$$

$$=\frac Ag(P_0+P_{\mathrm{atm}})(e^{\rho_0gh/2P_0}-1)\tag{4.9}$$

### (b)

$$P_i(z)=P_{\mathrm{atm}}+\frac{\rho_0}2gz\tag{4.10}$$

$$P(z)=(P_0+P_{\mathrm{atm}})e^{\rho_0gz/2P_0}-P_0\tag{4.11}$$

$$\approx P_0\left(1+\frac{P_{\mathrm{atm}}}{P_0}\right)\left[1+\frac{\rho_0gz}{2P_0}+\left(\frac{\rho_0gz}{2P_0}\right)^2\frac12\right]-P_0\tag{4.12}$$

$$\Delta P=P(z)-P_i(z)\tag{4.13}$$

$$=\frac{(\rho_0gz)^2}{8P_0}+\frac{P_{\mathrm{atm}}}{P_0}\frac{\rho_0gz}2+\frac{P_{\mathrm{atm}}}2\left(\frac{\rho_0gz}{2P_0}\right)^2\tag{4.14}$$

which is correct upto second order in $\rho_0gz/2P_0$.

$$\Delta P\approx\frac{P_{\mathrm{atm}}}{P_0}\frac{\rho_0gz}2\tag{4.15}$$

which is correct upto first order in $\rho_0gz/2P_0$.

**Both Eqs. (4.14) and (4.15) (mentioning order of approximation) gain full credit.**

problems.title: Parallel metallic rails
problems.statement:
A pair of long parallel metallic rails of negligible resistance and separation $w$ are placed horizontally. A horizontal metal rod (dark thick line) of mass $M$ and resistance $R$ is placed perpendicularly onto the rails at one end (as shown). A uniform magnetic field $B$ exists perpendicular to the plane of the paper (pointing into the page). One end of the rail track is connected to a key ($K$) and a capacitor of capacitance $C$ charged to voltage $V_0$. At $t=0$ the key is closed. Neglect friction and self inductance of the loop.

[[figure:p5-rails]]

parts.label: a)
parts.statement:
What is the final speed ($v_{\mathrm{final}}$) attained by the rod?

**Summary answer box:** $v_{\mathrm{final}}=$ [blank].

parts.label: b)
parts.statement:
Consider the ratio $r$ of the maximum kinetic energy attained by the rod to the energy initially stored in the capacitor. What is $r_{\max}$, the maximum possible value of $r$, by appropriately choosing $B$?

**Summary answer box:** $r_{\max}=$ [blank].

parts.label: c)
parts.statement:
Let $M=10.0\ \mathrm{kg}$, $w=0.10\ \mathrm m$, $V_0=1.00\times10^4\ \mathrm V$ and a bank of capacitors ensures that $C=1.00\ \mathrm F$. If $r=r_{\max}$, calculate the value of $v_{\mathrm{final}}$.

**Summary answer box:** $v_{\mathrm{final}}(r=r_{\max})=$ [blank].

Detailed answers can be found on page numbers: [blank].

figures.alt: Entire native rails, thick rod, capacitor polarity, switch K, field into page, w dimension and full circuit.

solution.statement:
### (a)

At $t=0$, $Q_0=CV_0$. At any instant, $\dot Q=-I$, where $Q$ is the charge on capacitor and $I$ is the current in RC circuit. From Newton’s second law and Lorentz force,

$$m\frac{dv}{dt}=IwB\tag{5.1}$$

$$=-\dot QwB\tag{5.2}$$

Induced emf in the circuit is $Bwv$. From KVL,

$$\frac QC=IR+Bwv\tag{5.3}$$

$$=-\dot QR+Bwv\tag{5.4}$$

Differentiating Eq. (5.4) and using Eq. (5.2)

$$\ddot Q=-\frac1{RC}\dot Q-\frac{B^2w^2}{mR}\dot Q\tag{5.5}$$

$$=-\dot Q\left[\frac1{RC}+\frac{B^2w^2}{mR}\right]\tag{5.6}$$

$$\ddot Q=-\frac{\dot Q}\tau\quad\text{where}\quad\frac1\tau=\frac1{RC}+\frac{B^2w^2}{mR}\tag{5.7}$$

$$\log\left(\frac{\dot Q}{\dot Q_0}\right)=-\frac t\tau\quad\text{where}\quad\dot Q_0=I(t=0)=-\frac{V_0}R\tag{5.8}$$

$$\dot Q=-\frac{V_0}R e^{-t/\tau}\tag{5.9}$$

Combining Eqs. (5.2) and (5.9)

$$m\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{V_oBw}R e^{-t/\tau}\tag{5.10}$$

$$\int_0^{v_{\mathrm{final}}}m\,dv=\int_0^\infty\frac{V_0Bw}R e^{-t/\tau}\,dt\tag{5.11}$$

$$mv_{\mathrm{final}}=\left.\frac{BwV_0}R(-\tau)e^{-t/\tau}\right|_0^\infty\tag{5.12}$$

$$=\frac{BwV_0\tau}R\tag{5.13}$$

$$v_{\mathrm{final}}=\frac{BwCV_0}{m+B^2w^2c}\tag{5.14}$$

**Source note:** The native question uses rod mass $M$; the native derivation uses $m$. Printed Eq. (5.8) identifies $\dot Q_0$ with $I(t=0)$ although the preceding text states $\dot Q=-I$. Eq. (5.10) prints $V_o$ with letter $o$, and Eq. (5.14) prints lowercase $c$ in its denominator while the capacitance elsewhere is $C$. All original notation and equalities are retained.

### (b)

$$r=\frac{mv_{\max}^2/2}{CV_0^2/2}\tag{5.15}$$

$$=\frac{x}{(1+x)^2}\quad\text{where}\quad x=\frac{B^2w^2C}m\tag{5.16}$$

$r$ has a maximum value of $\frac14$ at $x=1$.

$$r_{\max}=1/4\tag{5.17}$$

### (c)

For $r_{\max}$,

$$\frac{B^2w^2C}m=1\Rightarrow B=31.6\ \mathrm T\tag{5.18}$$

$$v_{\max}=1.58\times10^3\ \mathrm{m/s}\tag{5.19}$$

problems.title: A Diesel cycle
problems.statement:
Consider $n$ moles of a monoatomic non-ideal (realistic) gas. Its equation of state may be described by the van der Waal’s equation

$$\left(P+\frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)\left(\frac Vn-b\right)=RT$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants and other symbols have their usual meanings. The internal energy change of a realistic gas can be given by

$$dU=C_VdT+\left\{T\left(\frac{dP}{dT}\right)_V-P\right\}dV$$

As indicated in the above expression, the derivative of pressure is taken at constant volume. We take one mole of the gas ($n=1$) through a Diesel cycle (ABCDA) as shown in the following $P$-$V$ diagram (diagram is not to scale). During the whole cycle assume that the molar heat capacity at constant volume ($C_V$) remains constant at $3R/2$. Path AB and CD are reversible adiabats.

[[figure:p6-pv]]

parts.label: a)
parts.statement:
Obtain the temperature at B ($T_B$) in terms of temperature at A ($T_A$), $V_A$, $V_B$ and constants only.

**Summary answer box:** $T_B=$ [blank].

parts.label: b)
parts.statement:
Let temperature at A to be $T_A=100.00\ \mathrm K$, $V_A=8.00\ \mathrm l$, $V_B=1.00\ \mathrm l$, $V_C=2.00\ \mathrm l$, $a=1.355\ \mathrm{l^2\cdot atm/mol^2}$, and $b=0.0313\ \mathrm{l/mol}$. Calculate the highest temperature reached during the whole cycle.

**Summary answer box:** Highest temperature = [blank].

parts.label: c)
parts.statement:

**Summary answer box:** Value of $\eta=$ [blank].

parts.label: d)
parts.statement:

solution.statement:
### (a)

$$dU=C_VdT+\left\{\frac{RT}{V-b}-P\right\}dV$$

AB and CD are reversible adiabats, hence entropy change during these processes are zero.

$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{AB}}=\Delta S_{\mathrm{CD}}=\int_A^B\frac{dQ}T=\int_C^D\frac{dQ}T=0\tag{6.1}$$

$$\int_A^B\frac{dQ}T=\int\frac{C_V}T\,dT+\int\frac R{V-b}\,dV=0\tag{6.2}$$

$$C_V\ln\frac{T_B}{T_A}=-R\ln\left(\frac{V_B-b}{V_A-b}\right)\tag{6.3}$$

$$T_B=T_A\left(\frac{V_B-b}{V_A-b}\right)^{-R/C_V}=T_A\left(\frac{V_B-b}{V_A-b}\right)^{-2/3}\tag{6.4}$$

### (b)

Highest temperature during cycle is at $T_C$.

$$T_B=407.5\ \mathrm K\tag{6.5}$$

which gives, from van der Waal equation

$$P_B=33.18\ \mathrm{atm}=P_C\tag{6.6}$$

$$\Rightarrow T_C=803.76\ \mathrm K\approx804\ \mathrm K\tag{6.7}$$

Different value of $T_C$ (within a range) obtained due to reasonable roundoff in previous step(s) will be credited.

### (c)

$$dQ_{\mathrm{in}}=dQ_{\mathrm{BC}}=dU+P_BdV\tag{6.8}$$

$$=C_VdT+\frac{RT}{V-b}\,dV\tag{6.9}$$

$$=C_VdT+\left(P+\frac a{V^2}\right)dV\tag{6.10}$$

$$Q_{\mathrm{in}}=C_V(T_C-T_B)+P_B(V_C-V_B)-\left.\frac aV\right|_{V_B}^{V_C}\tag{6.11}$$

$$Q_{\mathrm{out}}=Q_{\mathrm{DA}}=C_V(T_A-T_D)\tag{6.12}$$

$$\eta=1-\frac{Q_{\mathrm{out}}}{Q_{\mathrm{in}}}=67.7\%\approx68\%\tag{6.13}$$

Different value of $\eta$ (within a range) obtained due to reasonable roundoff in previous step(s) will be credited.

### (d)

$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{BC}}=\int\frac{dQ}{dT}=\int\frac{C_VdT}T+\int\frac R{V-b}\,dV\tag{6.14}$$

$$=C_V\ln\frac{T_C}{T_B}+R\ln\frac{V_C-b}{V_B-b}\tag{6.15}$$

$$=1.73R=\Delta S_{\mathrm{DA}}\tag{6.16}$$

[[figure:p6-key-ts]]

[[figure:p6-key-vt]]

**Source note:** Eq. (6.12) prints $C_V(T_A-T_D)$ for $Q_{\mathrm{out}}$, while Eq. (6.13) gives a positive 67.7% efficiency with $1-Q_{\mathrm{out}}/Q_{\mathrm{in}}$. Eq. (6.14) prints $dQ/dT$ in its first integral rather than the $dQ/T$ used earlier. Eq. (6.16) prints positive $\Delta S_{\mathrm{DA}}=\Delta S_{\mathrm{BC}}$, whereas the native T-S plot shows DA returning toward smaller entropy. Native equations, values, arrows and graph labels remain literal. Both key plots label $T_C$ as803 K, whereas Eq. (6.7) rounds803.76 K to804 K.

solution.statement:
### (a)

$$V_T=\frac{mg(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)}b\tag{7.1}$$

$$S(t)=V_T\left[t-\frac mb\left(1-e^{-tb/m}\right)\right]\tag{7.2}$$

### (b)

$V_T=$ slope of the graph $=0.315\ \mathrm{m/s}$.
